lead: An electron in an atom is not a small ball; it is a wave with a shape. The Schrödinger equation is the rule that fixes that shape. Give it the particle's mass and the potential energy around it, and it returns the wavefunction. When the potential does not change with time, the equation splits into a space part and a rotating phase, and the space part hands you the allowed energies. Every energy level in physics — spectral lines, band gaps in semiconductors, laser transitions — comes out of this one equation.
prereq: You need: the wavefunction and its Born interpretation from 6.6, partial derivatives, and the classical wave equation from Unit 2, Oscillations and Waves.

blocks.text: The Schrödinger equation does for matter waves what Newton's second law does for a cricket ball. You supply the mass m of the particle and the potential energy V it sits in, and out comes the wavefunction ψ(x, t) of 6.6. No classical argument produces this equation. Schrödinger put it forward in 1926 as a postulate, and it survives because every experiment on atoms, electrons and nuclei agrees with its predictions.

blocks.where: ψ = ψ(x, t) is the wavefunction (complex); i = √−1; ℏ = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is the reduced Planck constant; m is the particle mass in kg; ∂²ψ/∂x² is the second derivative of ψ with respect to x; V = V(x, t) is the potential energy in joules. Each side of the equation has the units of an energy multiplied by ψ.

blocks.text: The form is guided by the classical energy relation for one particle, E = p²/2m + V. Replace the momentum p by the operator −iℏ ∂/∂x, replace the energy E by the operator iℏ ∂/∂t, and let both act on ψ. The result is the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, or TDSE.

blocks.where: Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator, the quantum operator for total energy (kinetic plus potential), in joules; the hat marks an operator rather than a number. In three dimensions ∂²/∂x² becomes the Laplacian ∇².

blocks.text: Take a potential that depends on x only, never on t. The TDSE then splits into two ordinary equations, one in x and one in t.

items: Guess a product solution ψ(x, t) = ψ(x)φ(t).
Substitute: iℏ ψ dφ/dt = φ [−(ℏ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² + Vψ].
Divide both sides by ψφ. The left side holds only t, the right side only x.
Two functions of different variables can be equal everywhere only if both equal one constant. Call it E, in joules.
Time part: iℏ dφ/dt = Eφ, so φ(t) = e^(−iEt/ℏ).
Space part: −(ℏ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² + V(x)ψ = Eψ, the time-independent Schrödinger equation (TISE).

blocks.where: ψ = ψ(x) is the spatial part of the wavefunction; E is the separation constant and turns out to be the total energy in joules. The equation says the Hamiltonian, acting on ψ, returns the same function multiplied by a number.

blocks.text: An equation of the shape Ĥψ = Eψ is an eigenvalue equation. ψ is an eigenfunction of Ĥ and E is the matching eigenvalue. Only particular pairs (ψ, E) survive the boundary conditions: ψ must be finite, single-valued and continuous everywhere, dψ/dx must be continuous wherever V is finite, and ψ must fall to zero at infinity for a bound particle. Those conditions, more than the equation itself, are what make energy discrete.

The full wavefunction is ψ(x)e^(−iEt/ℏ). Its probability density is |ψ|² = |ψ(x)|² × |e^(−iEt/ℏ)|² = |ψ(x)|², with no t in it. The complex phase rotates, but no measurable quantity moves. Such a state is a stationary state and it carries a definite energy E. Some syllabi call the TISE the steady-state equation.

sections.h3: Free particle: k, ω and E

blocks.text: Set V = 0 everywhere. The TISE becomes −(ℏ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² = Eψ, whose solutions are ψ(x) = A e^(ikx) + B e^(−ikx). Putting the time factor back gives travelling plane waves, one running each way.
ψ(x, t) = A e^(i(kx − ωt)) + B e^(−i(kx + ωt)),   E = ℏ²k²/(2m),   p = ℏk,   ω = E/ℏ
blocks.where: k = 2π/λ is the wave number in m⁻¹ and λ is the de Broglie wavelength in metres; A and B are the amplitudes of the right-going and left-going waves; p is momentum in kg·m/s; ω is angular frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: Energy grows as the square of the wave number: double k and E becomes four times larger. The phase velocity is ω/k = ℏk/2m, only half the particle speed. The group velocity dω/dk = ℏk/m = p/m is exactly the classical speed, the same result met in 6.4.

A single plane wave has the same |ψ|² at every x, so it cannot be normalised over infinite space. Physically it stands for a beam, normalised inside a large box, or for one component of a localised wave packet. Confining the particle instead of freeing it turns the continuous label k into a discrete set — that is the particle in a box, 6.8.

figure.caption: A time-independent potential lets the time-dependent equation split into a phase factor and a space equation; solving the space equation under the boundary conditions gives the allowed energies of the stationary states.

spec.title: From TDSE to steady state
spec.aria: The time-dependent Schrodinger equation separates when the potential is time-independent, giving the time-independent equation and energy eigenvalues for stationary states.

examples.question: A free electron moves in a region where V = 0 and has wave number k = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ m⁻¹. Using the time-independent Schrödinger equation, find its energy in joules and in electronvolts, and the angular frequency ω of its time factor. Take ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
steps: With V = 0 the TISE reads −(ℏ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² = Eψ.
Try ψ = A e^(ikx). Then dψ/dx = ikA e^(ikx) and d²ψ/dx² = −k²A e^(ikx) = −k²ψ.
Compute ℏ² = (1.055 × 10⁻³⁴)² = 1.113 × 10⁻⁶⁸ J²·s² and k² = (1.0 × 10¹⁰)² = 1.0 × 10²⁰ m⁻². Numerator ℏ²k² = 1.113 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J²·s²·m⁻².
The time factor is e^(−iEt/ℏ), so ω = E/ℏ = 6.11 × 10⁻¹⁹ ÷ 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.79 × 10¹⁵ rad/s.
examples.answer: E = 6.11 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.81 eV, and the angular frequency is ω = 5.79 × 10¹⁵ rad/s.
examples.check:
hbar = 1.055e-34
m = 9.11e-31
k = 1.0e10
E = hbar**2 * k**2 / (2 * m)
print(round(E / 1e-19, 2))
print(round(E / 1.602e-19, 2))
print(round((E / hbar) / 1e15, 2))

traps: Using the time-independent equation when V depends on time. The separation step fails, the state is not stationary, and you must return to the TDSE.
Dropping the boundary conditions. Ĥψ = Eψ admits solutions for a whole range of E; only those that are finite, single-valued, continuous, and vanish at infinity for a bound state are physical.
Sign and derivative slips: the kinetic term carries a minus sign, −(ℏ²/2m)∇², and the left side of the TDSE is iℏ ∂ψ/∂t, not −iℏ ∂ψ/∂t.
Mixing up ω and ν. ω = E/ℏ in rad/s while ν = E/h in Hz; the missing factor of 2π is the usual lost mark.
Reading e^(−iEt/ℏ) as motion. The phase rotates but |ψ|² stays constant; any observable change needs a superposition of at least two stationary states.

quiz.q: Write the one-dimensional time-dependent Schrödinger equation and name each symbol.
quiz.a: iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = −(ℏ²/2m) ∂²ψ/∂x² + Vψ. ψ is the wavefunction, ℏ = h/2π the reduced Planck constant, m the mass, V the potential energy, and i = √−1.

quiz.q: Why does a stationary state give a probability density that does not change with time?
quiz.a: The full function is ψ(x)e^(−iEt/ℏ). Its modulus squared is |ψ(x)|² × |e^(−iEt/ℏ)|² = |ψ(x)|², because the phase factor has modulus 1 at every instant. The phase turns in the complex plane but the density stays fixed.

quiz.q: A free electron has k = 2.0 × 10¹⁰ m⁻¹ with V = 0. Find its energy in eV. Use ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
quiz.a: E = ℏ²k²/(2m). Doubling k multiplies the earlier result by 4: ℏ²k² = 4.452 × 10⁻⁴⁸, 2m = 1.822 × 10⁻³⁰, so E = 2.44 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = 15.3 eV.

quiz.q: A student applies the time-independent Schrödinger equation to a particle in a potential V(t) = V₀ sin ωt. Explain what is wrong and what should replace it.
quiz.a: The separation ψ(x)φ(t) needs V to depend on x only; with V(t) the two sides of the divided equation cannot both be constant, so no stationary state exists and E is not sharp. The full TDSE must be used, and the particle can be driven between energy levels.

quiz.q: State two differences between Ĥψ = Eψ and iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ.
quiz.a: The first holds only when V has no time dependence and it is an eigenvalue equation whose solutions are stationary states; the second holds always and gives the time evolution of any wavefunction.

quiz.q: For a free particle, why can E take any positive value but no negative value?
quiz.a: E = ℏ²k²/(2m) with k real, so E ≥ 0 runs over all positive values. A negative E would need an imaginary k, giving a real exponential that cannot be normalised over all space, so no such free state exists.

quiz.q: An electron sits in a region of constant potential V = 2.0 eV with total energy E = 3.81 eV. What is its kinetic energy and its wave number?

beyond: Not for the exam. Research groups integrate the TDSE every day: a femtosecond laser pulse striking a molecule, an electron driven by a terahertz field, a superconducting qubit being flipped. Exact solution in three dimensions is far too heavy, so codes use split-operator or Crank–Nicolson schemes on a grid, and time-dependent perturbation theory when the drive is weak. Quantum chemistry software solving a molecular orbital is really solving a large time-independent eigenvalue problem of the same Ĥψ = Eψ type. Search next for time-dependent perturbation theory, Fermi's golden rule, and the split-operator method.
